paragraphs.heading: The heaviest water in the sea
paragraphs.text: Antarctic bottom water is a water mass of the Southern Ocean, the sea that rings Antarctica. It is very cold, between −0.8 and 2 °C, and holds 34.6 to 35.0 g of salt in each kilogram of water. As the densest water mass in the oceans, it fills everything below 4000 m in each basin linked to the Southern Ocean at that depth. Across most of the southern hemisphere it lies underneath the other bottom and middle-depth waters. Its densest part is called Weddell Sea Bottom Water.

paragraphs.heading: Born in holes in the ice
paragraphs.text: This water starts life at the surface, in openings in the sea ice along the Antarctic coast. Cold winds blowing off the continent push newly made sea ice out to sea, leaving patches of open water called polynyas. The bare water meets the freezing winter air, so still more ice forms there. In one season these coastal polynyas can make up to a tenth of all Southern Ocean sea ice, around 2,000 km³. The water sinks in four places: the Ross Sea, the Weddell Sea, the waters off the Adélie Coast, and the area near Cape Darnley.

paragraphs.heading: How it sinks
paragraphs.text: When sea ice grows, it leaves its salt behind in the water below, a process called brine rejection. At the same time the winter air chills that water. Saltier and colder water is heavier, so it pours down the continental slope and keeps moving north along the seafloor. Because it forms at the surface, this water trades large amounts of heat and gases with the air. Its sinking then ventilates the deep ocean. It starts out rich in oxygen compared with other deep waters, though the oxygen is used up over time.

paragraphs.heading: A slow trip north
paragraphs.text: Antarctic bottom water forms the lower branch of thermohaline circulation, the great overturning of the world's oceans. In the South Atlantic it travels north through the Vema Channel, a deep trench cut into the Rio Grande Rise. When it reaches the equator, about a third of it turns into the Guiana Basin. In the Indian Ocean it flows toward the equator through the Crozet–Kerguelen Gap at 2.5 Sv. The water needs 23 years just to get as far as that gap.

paragraphs.heading: A shield for the ice shelves
paragraphs.text: A major source of this bottom water is circumpolar deep water, a warm water mass found offshore. Coastal polynyas cool it into the denser bottom water. In doing so they keep that warm water from reaching the undersides of the floating ice shelves, which protects them from melting from below. In the Amundsen Sea, polynya activity has dropped so far that dense water hardly forms. The ice shelves next to it have begun to retreat and may be close to collapse.

paragraphs.heading: A slowing supply
paragraphs.text: Climate change and melting of the southern ice sheet have already slowed the making of this water, and the slowdown will likely go on. Its formation could stop completely as early as 2050, with dramatic effects on ocean circulation and weather around the world. Single events matter too: when the Mertz Glacier calved in February 2010, bottom water export near Adélie Land fell by up to 23%. Extra ice melt also left the bottom water fresher between 2011 and 2015.
